learningObjective: Trace how the deployed fraud policy determines which outcomes become labels, then identify why an independently reviewed sample must cover both allowed and declined transactions.
mediumRationale: A deterministic SVG is the smallest medium that can separate outcome labels from independent review labels, show the missing counterfactual after a decline, and connect both policy branches to a coverage-repair sample while guaranteeing readable labels in the narrow article column.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected after render testing: labelled branches expressed the semantics, but the complete graph shrank its smallest text to 6.95 CSS pixels, below a readable instructional size.
mediumComparison.svg: Selected: fixed narrow-column lanes preserve the action split, outcome states, and cross-policy audit sample with controlled text sizes and no runtime layout dependency.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected: a table could inventory label states, but it would obscure that the deployed policy creates those states and therefore shapes the next training set.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: changing the policy threshold could alter label coverage, but controls would add state while leaving the fundamental observability split unchanged.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: none of the reviewed sources contains this article-specific payment flow, and reuse permission for their figures was not established. No figure, layout, data, or wording is copied.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: the prose names label bias and random investigation, but readers must still mentally connect policy action, delayed chargeback observability, missing decline outcomes, and representative label acquisition.

pages.insight: The preceding classification-loss slide mentions focal loss for imbalanced data but contains no payment-fraud label process.
The classification-evaluation slide defines precision, recall, ROC, and the benefit-cost operating-point tradeoff, but assumes ground-truth labels are already observed.
The neighboring imbalanced binary-classification example shows why accuracy fails and why precision-recall tradeoffs matter, but does not question how positives and negatives were labeled.
The following calibration slide connects scores to confidence and rejection, but adds no treatment of delayed, missing, or policy-selected fraud outcomes.
The slide before data inspection contains general training notes and marks the boundary of the data-quality neighborhood.
The data-inspection slide explicitly asks readers to inspect imbalance, biases, the labeling process, and label noise, but provides no observation-flow model.
The adjacent training-skeleton slide discusses class-prior initialization and model sanity checks, not selective labels or counterfactual outcomes.
The project-setup slide asks whether false positives or false negatives cost more and how inference-time outcomes support evaluation.
The data-pipeline slide asks about annotation quality and cost, user feedback, class imbalance, distribution shift, and data bias, but does not show how a fraud policy controls outcome observability.
The following modeling slide moves from data questions to baseline model selection, marking the end of the relevant system-design neighborhood.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page local deck was indexed for fraud, chargeback, payment, anomaly, imbalance, precision-recall, active learning, selective labels, annotation, bias, and adversarial behavior. It contains no fraud- or chargeback-specific slide. Physical PDF pages 36-39, 57-59, and 165-167 were extracted independently and read as the complete nearest neighborhoods. They cover imbalanced evaluation, noisy-label inspection, asymmetric costs, and annotation questions, but never connect a deployed action to whether a later outcome can be observed. No deck image, wording, values, or layout is reused.

sources.title: The Selective Labels Problem: Evaluating Algorithmic Predictions in the Presence of Unobservables
sources.usage: Used as the foundational primary source to verify that decision-maker choices determine which instances receive outcomes, making the labelled subset non-random and ordinary evaluation potentially biased.
sources.license: The PMC record makes the article readable, but no permissive figure-reuse grant was relied on. No figure, text, application example, result, or layout is reproduced.

sources.title: From Biased Selective Labels to Pseudo-Labels: An Expectation-Maximization Framework for Learning from Biased Decisions
sources.usage: Used as a primary peer-reviewed source to cross-check that imputing policy-unobserved labels as negative can amplify labeling bias.
sources.license: PMLR papers are publicly available for scholarly use, but the visual does not adapt any paper figure, algorithm, experiment, prose, or visual structure.

sources.title: Reproducible Machine Learning for Credit Card Fraud Detection - Practical Handbook
sources.usage: Used as an authoritative fraud-detection textbook to verify score-threshold decisions, heavy class imbalance, unequal false-positive and false-negative costs, and the limits of accuracy for fraud evaluation.
sources.license: The handbook repository is Apache-2.0 licensed, but its plots, code, numerical examples, and prose are not reused. The implementation is an independently authored policy-label schematic.

sources.title: Payment fraud detection and approval rates
sources.usage: Used as payment-industry documentation to verify layered rules and ML, allow/challenge/decline actions, delayed disputes, and the coupled fraud-rate, false-positive, chargeback, and approval-rate tradeoffs.
sources.license: Stripe retains copyright in its documentation and no figure-reuse permission was identified. No prose, artwork, metrics, or page structure is copied.

sourceReview.notes: The visual distinguishes two evidence mechanisms. Outcome labels follow the deployed action: an allowed payment may later produce a chargeback or mature without one, while a declined payment has no realized payment outcome and must not be called legitimate. Independent analyst or adjudication review can sample both policy branches and create a separate label source, subject to review quality. That sample supports coverage checks and base-rate or calibration estimates; it does not magically reveal every declined transaction's counterfactual payment outcome. Chargebacks are also delayed and imperfect, so the diagram labels a mature no-chargeback outcome as a noisy negative rather than guaranteed legitimacy.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete fraud-system article, indexed all 214 deck pages and inspected three exact neighboring slide clusters, then checked foundational selective-label research, a recent peer-reviewed treatment, an authoritative fraud handbook, and payment-industry documentation before selecting an original policy-to-label flow.

implementation.accessibility: The SVG provides a linked title and complete description. Every policy action, outcome state, missing-label warning, sampling path, and training result is directly labelled; box boundaries, lane headings, solid arrows, and labelled dashed audit paths carry the lesson without color. The established plot-panel primitive scales the 360-unit viewBox without a minimum width for controlled readability at 390 CSS pixels; shared theme tokens maintain dark-mode contrast and print uses a light high-contrast palette.
